title: The Zhabdrung and Bhutan's Dzong System
meta_description: How Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal built Bhutan from 1616: the dual system, the great dzongs of Simtokha, Punakha, Paro and Trongsa, and the road to the monarchy.
summary: Bhutan as a single state begins with Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal, a Drukpa lama who arrived from Tibet in 1616. He unified the western valleys, set up a dual system of religious and civil rule, and built dzongs that were fortress, monastery and government office at once. Many still work that way today.

sections.heading: A lama from Ralung, 1616
paras: Ngawang Namgyal was born in 1594 into the ruling family of the Drukpa school of Tibetan Buddhism, whose seat was the monastery of Ralung in Tibet. A dispute arose over who was the rightful head of the Drukpa lineage. A rival claimant had the backing of the powerful ruler of Tsang in central Tibet, and facing arrest, in 1616 Ngawang Namgyal left Tibet and crossed south into the valleys that are now western Bhutan.

At the time those valleys were ruled by rival local lords and lamas of several Buddhist schools. Over the next three decades Ngawang Namgyal brought them under one authority, fought off several invasions from Tibet, and took the title Zhabdrung, roughly 'at whose feet one submits'. The Drukpa name gave the country its own: Druk Yul, the land of the thunder dragon. Bhutanese still call the Zhabdrung the founder of the nation.

sections.heading: The dual system of government
paras: The Zhabdrung's most lasting idea was a dual system of rule, called chhoesi. Religious affairs were placed under the Je Khenpo, the chief abbot, who led the monastic body. Civil affairs were placed under the Desi, a lay ruler who managed government, taxes and defence. The Zhabdrung himself stood above both.

Below the Desi, regional governors called penlops ran the great regions, and district officers ran each valley from its dzong. The system lasted, in one form or another, until the monarchy in 1907, and parts of it survive. The Je Khenpo still heads the Central Monastic Body today, and many dzongs still house both monks and district officials under one roof.

For a visitor, the clearest sign of the dual system is the way a dzong is laid out. In a big dzong such as Punakha or Paro, one courtyard is ringed by government offices, where people come to pay taxes, register land or meet the district officials. Another courtyard belongs to the monks, with temples, prayer halls and their living quarters. Your guide will show you where one ends and the other begins, and what is kept in the tall central tower, the utse, which usually holds some of the dzong's most important chapels.

sections.heading: Fortress, monastery and office
paras: A dzong is not quite a fort, a monastery or a town hall; it is all three. Each was built on a strategic spot, a ridge, a river confluence or the mouth of a valley, with high, whitewashed walls that slope inward and small windows at the bottom. Inside, the space is usually split: roughly half for administration, such as the governor's offices, and half for religion, with temples and monks' quarters around a courtyard and a central tower.

The first was Simtokha Dzong, built in 1629 just south of present-day Thimphu, guarding the road between the Thimphu valley and the east. Punakha Dzong followed in 1637–38, at the meeting of the Pho Chhu and Mo Chhu rivers, and became the seat of government until the capital moved to Thimphu in 1955. Wangdue Phodrang Dzong was founded in 1638, Rinpung Dzong at Paro in 1644–46, and Trongsa Dzong, on its ridge in central Bhutan, in 1647.

sections.heading: The major dzongs and how they are used now
paras: The table lists the dzongs most visitors see, with the founding dates given in standard histories. Several were damaged by fires and earthquakes and rebuilt, so what you walk through is often later work on the Zhabdrung's plan. Entry for regional and international tourists is usually Nu 500 per adult, indicative 2026, and opening hours are limited when offices are working; check current status before you travel.

sections.heading: The secret of 1651
paras: The Zhabdrung died in 1651. His officials did not announce it. For about half a century, 54 years by the usual count, the government said that he had entered a long meditation retreat, and orders continued to be issued in his name. The reason was political: the state he had built rested on his personal authority, and there was no agreed successor. Announcing his death risked civil war.

When the truth finally came out, the problem it had hidden returned. Through the 18th and 19th centuries the Desi was often weak, and the real power lay with the regional penlops of Paro and Trongsa, who fought each other for control. Punakha Dzong holds the Machey Lhakhang, a chapel that keeps the Zhabdrung's embalmed body; visitors normally see it only from outside, but your guide will point it out, and it explains why Punakha matters so much to Bhutanese.

sections.heading: From Trongsa Penlop to king, 1907
paras: Trongsa Dzong controlled the only east to west route through central Bhutan, and whoever held it controlled much of the country. In the 19th century the Trongsa Penlops of the Wangchuck family became the strongest power in Bhutan. In 1865, after the Duar War, Bhutan signed the Treaty of Sinchula with British India and gave up the Duars, the strip of plains that is now the Dooars of West Bengal and Assam.

Ugyen Wangchuck, Penlop of Trongsa, won a decisive civil war battle at Changlimithang in Thimphu in the 1880s and became the country's dominant figure. He acted as an intermediary for the British expedition to Lhasa in 1904 and was knighted the following year. On 17 December 1907, at Punakha Dzong, an assembly of monks, officials and leading families chose him as the first hereditary king, the Druk Gyalpo. Bhutan celebrates 17 December as National Day.

sections.heading: Toward a constitutional monarchy
paras: Five Wangchuck kings have ruled since 1907. The Third King, Jigme Dorji Wangchuck, set up the National Assembly in 1953 and moved the capital to Thimphu. The Fourth King, Jigme Singye Wangchuck, crowned in 1974, began handing power away from the throne.

In 1998 he devolved executive power to an elected Council of Ministers. Work on a written constitution began in 2001. He abdicated in December 2006 in favour of his son, Jigme Khesar Namgyel Wangchuck, who was crowned in 2008. The first parliamentary elections were held that year, and the Constitution was adopted on 18 July 2008. The dzongs remained at the centre: the Fifth King married at Punakha Dzong in 2011, in the building the Zhabdrung began almost four centuries earlier.

sections.heading: Seeing the story on the ground
paras: You can follow this history on an ordinary Thimphu, Punakha and Paro trip, with a licensed guide and the usual dzong entry fees of about Nu 500 per adult, indicative 2026. These are the places where each chapter is easiest to picture.
list: Simtokha Dzong, a few kilometres south of Thimphu: the Zhabdrung's first dzong of 1629, small enough to understand in half an hour.
Tashichho Dzong, Thimphu: the seat of government and the king's office today; visitors are usually allowed in the evening after offices close.
Changlimithang, Thimphu: the national stadium and archery ground stand on the site of Ugyen Wangchuck's battle.
Punakha Dzong: the Zhabdrung's capital, the 1907 coronation hall and the winter home of the monks, best seen when the jacaranda trees flower in spring.
Rinpung Dzong, Paro: walk down from the dzong to the old covered bridge over the Paro Chhu.
Trongsa Dzong and the Ta Dzong watchtower above it: the seat of the Penlops, on the long drive to Bumthang.

faqs.a: Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal (1594–1651) was a lama of the Drukpa school who came to Bhutan from Ralung in Tibet in 1616. He unified the western valleys under one government, fought off invasions from Tibet, and set up a dual system with a chief abbot for religion and a lay Desi for civil rule. He also built the first great dzongs, and Bhutanese regard him as the founder of the nation.

faqs.q: What is a dzong in Bhutan
faqs.a: A dzong is a fortified building that serves as fortress, monastery and administrative centre at once. Typically about half the rooms are offices of the district government and half are temples and monks' quarters, arranged around courtyards and a central tower. Most districts are run from their dzong. Simtokha Dzong of 1629 was the first built by the Zhabdrung.

faqs.q: Which is the oldest dzong in Bhutan
faqs.a: Simtokha Dzong, built by Zhabdrung Ngawang Namgyal in 1629 just south of Thimphu, is usually described as the first dzong of unified Bhutan and is among the oldest surviving. It now houses a Dzongkha language institute. Some dzongs, such as Trongsa and Tashichho, stand on sites with older temples, but Simtokha is the first built as a Zhabdrung dzong.

Punakha Dzong, built in 1637–38 by the Zhabdrung, was Bhutan's seat of government until the capital moved to Thimphu in 1955. Ugyen Wangchuck was chosen as the first king there on 17 December 1907, and the Fifth King's wedding was held there in 2011. It keeps the Zhabdrung's embalmed body in the Machey Lhakhang and is the winter seat of the Je Khenpo.

faqs.q: Why was the Zhabdrung's death kept secret
faqs.a: When the Zhabdrung died in 1651, officials feared the new state would break apart without his authority, as there was no agreed successor. They announced that he had entered a long meditation retreat and kept issuing orders in his name for about half a century. When the death became known, rivalries among regional governors returned and lasted until the monarchy in 1907.

faqs.q: What is the dual system of government in Bhutan
faqs.a: The dual system, chhoesi, was set up by the Zhabdrung in the 17th century. Religious affairs were led by the Je Khenpo, the chief abbot, and civil affairs by the Desi, a lay ruler. Regional penlops and district officers worked under the Desi from the dzongs. The Je Khenpo still heads the Central Monastic Body, and dzongs still hold both monks and officials.

faqs.q: How did the Wangchuck dynasty begin
faqs.a: The Wangchucks were Penlops of Trongsa, rulers of central Bhutan, in the 19th century. Ugyen Wangchuck won the battle of Changlimithang in the 1880s, became the most powerful figure in the country, and on 17 December 1907 was chosen as the first hereditary king at Punakha Dzong by an assembly of monks, officials and leading families. That date is now Bhutan's National Day.

Yes, most major dzongs open their courtyards to visitors, usually with an entry fee of about Nu 500 per adult, indicative 2026, and with a licensed guide. Hours are limited because the dzongs are working offices and monasteries. Dress modestly with long sleeves and long trousers or skirts, remove caps, and do not photograph inside shrine rooms. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is Trongsa Dzong known for
faqs.a: Trongsa Dzong, built in 1647 on the site of a temple founded in 1543, controlled the main east to west route through central Bhutan. Its governors, the Penlops of Trongsa, became the strongest power in the country in the 19th century, and the first king, Ugyen Wangchuck, held that post before 1907. Today it houses district offices, about 200 monks and a printing house.
